100 Days of Deception Review: Kim You-jung & Jinyoung Shine | K-Drama Review | t2ONLINE

 K-Drama 
 Screen Kim You-jung plays a street thief drawn into Korea’s independence movement in 100 Days of Deception
 By Ankita Chandra 
 Published: 26 Oct 2026, 12:00AM | 4 min read Kim You-jung and Jinyoung in 100 Days of Deception
 Advertisement Genre : Historical drama, revolution 
 Where to watch: Netflix 
 You will love it if you love: 
 Political strategies 
 Colonial history 
 Revolutionaries in hiding 
 Strangers-to-lovers arcs 
 Buried pasts 
 t2 rating : 4/5
 If there were a ‘shape-shifter’ award for versatile talent in K-drama, Kim You-jung would definitely be among the strongest contenders. Less than a year after her chilling portrayal of a sociopath in Viki’s psycho-thriller Dear X , the actor is back with another rare portrayal, this time as a pickpocket operating as a revolutionary spy in Japan-ruled Korea in the early twentieth century.
 The character features as the main protagonist in Netflix’s recent release 100 Days of Deception . The drama tells a semi-historical tale of a group of Koreans hatching an elaborate assassination plot to kill the Japanese governor-general ruling a part of Joseon, the name by which the administrators referred to modern-day Korea. Set against the backdrop of the 1932 League of Nations negotiations involving Japan, the drama also stars GOT7 member Jinyoung, who plays Sato Hideo, the adopted Korean son of the governor-general, who works as an interpreter at the Japanese administrative office.
 The production invests a lot of effort in faithfully building the colonial backdrop against which the story unfolds. The Japanese government’s dependence on the Western media and its need for validation from the white colonisers who had conquered other parts of the globe are evident in the Anglicised fashion, lifestyle and amenities adopted by the administrators. Trench coats, bowler hats, aristocratic train coaches and lavish houses with gardens abound, giving the show its historical feel while also creating the cosmopolitan ambience that connects Asian politics with the West.
 In contrast to the picture-perfect lives led by Japanese government officials and their subordinates, the world of the Korean subjects is filled with dirt, waste and crushed hopes. Ga-kyung (Kim You-jung), who works as a pickpocket alongside many other helpless youths under a corrupt guardian figure, has seen even worse times as a child. She used to work as a housemaid in a white missionary’s house, where the family members severely exploited her and did not even allow her basic sustenance. Now picking pockets as a young woman, she dreams of escaping to America, a land that signifies freedom to her.
 Ga-kyung’s life changes when she accidentally finds herself embroiled in a bloodbath amid gunshots at the house where the revolutionary So-ran and journalist Philip have planned to assassinate the Japanese governor-general. When their attempt fails owing to the sudden appearance of So-ran’s husband, who tries to shoot Sato Hideo (Jinyoung), the governor-general’s adopted son, the police suspect So-ran, Philip and Ga-kyung. The latter poses as the housemaid at the residence to avoid suspicion.
 Witnessing her English-speaking skills and presence of mind, the revolutionaries, led by So-ran, decide to place her as a spy in the Japanese administrative office, promising to send her to America if she can help them with their mission. Ga-kyung’s immediate superior at the office is Hideo, who is also desperate to recover a seemingly old and useless pawnshop ticket from his wallet, which is in Ga-kyung’s possession, although she is reluctant to admit that she was the one who stole it. Will Ga-kyung succeed in bringing about the revolution for Korean independence? And what secret is Hideo hiding behind his mysterious pawn ticket? These questions will possibly be answered in the next episodes, which drop every Saturday and Sunday on Netflix. 
 Characters we treasure… 
 Kim You-jung as Lee Ga-kyung: 
   From a cold, elite CEO to a  manipulative sociopath, You- jung  has proven her versatility  across character tropes in an  acting career that already spans  more than two decades, despite  her being just 27. Ga-kyung is  a unique character, travelling  from the desperation of poverty  through the street-smartness  of being a pickpocket to the  solemn secrecy of a spy leading a  revolution. As usual, You-jung’s  precise expressions and confident  transitions between the various  contexts of the character’s life  become the anchoring force of the  plot. She is indeed the thread that  binds the complicated political  and personal layers of the plot  together. 
 Jinyoung as Sato Hideo: 
 In contrast to You-jung’s street-smart Ga-kyung is Jinyoung’s gentlemanly, diplomatic Hideo, a character who combines the commanding persona of an administrator with the soft heart of a helpless child who has spent his life looking for a place to belong. Like You-jung, Jinyoung has earned a reputation for versatility across genres, from psychological and legal dramas to heart-touching romances. The actor portrays Hideo with just the right balance of administrative swagger and the emotional vulnerability of a young man who has been compelled to internalise an alien culture for his survival.
